text: The International Space Station (ISS) is a large space station assembled and maintained in low Earth orbit by five space agencies—NASA (United States), Roscosmos (Russia), ESA (Europe), JAXA (Japan), and CSA (Canada)—through a collaboration involving their contractors. As the largest space station ever built, it primarily serves as a platform for conducting scientific experiments in microgravity and studying the space environment. The station is divided into two main segments: the Russian Orbital Segment (ROS), developed by Roscosmos, and the US Orbital Segment (USOS), built by NASA, ESA, JAXA, and CSA. A key structural component is the Integrated Truss Structure, which connects the station’s solar panels and radiators to its pressurized modules, which support functions such as scientific research, crew habitation, storage, spacecraft control, and airlock operations. The ISS has eight docking and berthing ports for visiting spacecraft and orbits Earth at an average altitude of 400 kilometres (250 miles), completing one orbit every 93 minutes and 15.5 orbits per day. The station originated from the combination of the United States' Space Station Freedom and the Soviet Union's Mir-2, with the first module launched in 1998 and long-term occupancy beginning on 2 November 2000 with the arrival of the Expedition 1 crew. Since then, the ISS has remained continuously inhabited for 25 years and 78 days, the longest continuous human presence in space. As of August 2025, 290 individuals from 26 countries have visited the station. Future plans include adding at least one module, Axiom Space's Payload Power Thermal Module, and the station is expected to remain operational until the end of 2030, after which it will be de-orbited using the US Deorbit Vehicle. The concept of international space collaboration began in the early 1970s, culminating in the 1975 Apollo–Soyuz Test Project, the first docking of spacecraft from two different spacefaring nations. Concepts such as International Skylab, Skylab-Salyut, and Shuttle-Salyut were proposed but abandoned due to falling budgets and rising Cold War tensions. In the early 1980s, NASA planned Space Station Freedom, with ESA approving the Columbus laboratory by 1987 and Japan announcing the Japanese Experiment Module (JEM or Kibō) in 1985. In 1985, ESA science ministers approved the Columbus program, which aimed to evolve into a full-fledged European orbital outpost. Rising costs in the early 1990s led Congress to demand increased international participation to avoid cancellation of Freedom. Meanwhile, the USSR began constructing modules for Mir-2 in the mid-1980s, but the collapse of the Soviet Union led to its significant downsizing and potential cancellation. American and Russian officials then proposed combining the two projects. In September 1993, U.S. Vice President Al Gore and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin announced plans for a new space station, which became the International Space Station, and agreed on the Shuttle–Mir program for American Shuttle docking with Mir. Originally intended as a laboratory, observatory, and factory with roles in transportation, maintenance, and as a staging base for future missions to the Moon, Mars, and asteroids, not all initial uses have been realized. The 2010 United States National Space Policy expanded the ISS’s roles to include commercial, diplomatic, and educational purposes. The ISS supports scientific research with power, data, cooling, and crew available for experiments, including small uncrewed spacecraft for zero gravity and space exposure studies, with long-term studies possible due to human researcher access. Experiments are conducted in fields such as astrobiology, astronomy, physical sciences, materials science, space weather, meteorology, and human research, including space medicine and life sciences. Scientists on Earth can access data and suggest modifications, and resupply missions allow routine hardware launches. Crews conduct expeditions of several months, providing about 160 man-hours per week with a six-member crew, though much of this time is spent on station maintenance. A notable experiment is the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS), which detects dark matter and other cosmic phenomena; NASA considers it as important as the Hubble Space Telescope. On 3 April 2013, scientists reported hints of dark matter detected by AMS, noting an unexplained excess of high-energy positrons in cosmic rays. The space environment is hostile, featuring intense radiation, high vacuum, extreme temperatures, and microgravity; extremophiles and tardigrades can survive in dry conditions. Medical research on the ISS studies long-term effects such as muscle atrophy, bone loss, and fluid shift, with data suggesting significant risks of fractures and movement problems for Mars missions. The National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI) conducts studies such as the Advanced Diagnostic Ultrasound in Microgravity, where astronauts perform ultrasound scans under remote expert guidance, with potential applications in Earth-based emergency and rural care. In August 2020, scientists reported that Deinococcus radiodurans bacteria survived for three years in space, supporting the panspermia hypothesis. Earth remote sensing, astronomy, and deep space research have increased since 2011 with the completion of the US Orbital Segment, including experiments on aerosols, ozone, lightning, oxides, the Sun, cosmic rays, cosmic dust, antimatter, and dark matter. Research also examines the effects of microgravity on plant and animal development, with NASA investigating microgravity’s impact on human-like tissues and protein crystals. Fluid physics studies in microgravity improve models of fluid behavior, especially for non-mixing fluids and low-temperature reactions, aiding understanding of superconductivity. Materials science research aims to improve Earth-based techniques, and studies on combustion in microgravity may enhance energy production and reduce emissions. The ISS provides a safe environment in low Earth orbit to test spacecraft systems for long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, offering experience in operations, maintenance, and repair. While the ISS addresses effects of weightlessness and radiation, ground-based simulations like MARS-500 address long-term isolation and confinement. In 2009, Sergey Krasnov of Roscosmos stated that international partnerships enhance space exploration success and safety, and in 2010, ESA Director-General Jean-Jacques Dordain proposed inviting China, India, and South Korea to join the ISS. NASA chief Charles Bolden stated in 2011 that any Mars mission would likely be global. However, U.S. federal legislation prevents NASA from cooperating with China without FBI and congressional approval. The ISS offers educational opportunities through student experiments, classroom activities, radio and email engagement, and free teaching materials from ESA. JAXA aims to inspire children to pursue craftsmanship and awareness of societal responsibilities, with experiments like "Seeds in Space" exploring mutations in sunflower seeds flown on the ISS. Cultural activities are also a major objective, with Tetsuo Tanaka noting that space resonates with people beyond science. Amateur Radio on the ISS (ARISS) is a volunteer program involving delegations from nine countries, enabling students worldwide to communicate with the crew via radio or speakerphone. In 2011, a documentary film titled First Orbit was released, matching the ISS orbit to Vostok 1 to film the view Yuri Gagarin experienced, combining it with original audio recordings from the Russian State Archive. In May 2013, commander Chris Hadfield filmed a music video of David Bowie's "Space Oddity" on the ISS, the first music video filmed in space. In November 2017, during Expedition 52/53, Paolo Nespoli recorded spoken voice content in English and Italian for use on Wikipedia, the first content made in space specifically for Wikipedia. In November 2021, a virtual reality exhibit called The Infinite featuring life aboard the ISS was announced. The ISS involves five space programs and fifteen countries and is the most politically and legally complex space exploration program in history, governed primarily by the 1998 Space Station Intergovernmental Agreement and subsequent agreements on jurisdiction and conduct. Brazil was invited to participate, to provide six hardware elements in exchange for utilization rights, but failed to deliver due to lack of funding and political priority and officially withdrew in 2007. Following the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, cooperation between Russia and other ISS partners has been questioned. Roscosmos Director General Dmitry Rogozin claimed that blocking cooperation would lead to an unguided de-orbit of the ISS impacting the U.S. or Europe, or even India or China—an untrue claim, as the ISS flies over latitudes between 51.6 degrees north and south. Rogozin later stated that normal relations could only resume after sanctions were lifted and proposed ending cooperation to the Russian government. NASA stated that, if needed, Northrop Grumman has offered a reboost capability to maintain the station’s orbit. On 26 July 2022, Yury Borisov, Rogozin’s successor, submitted plans to Russia for withdrawal from the program after 2024.

The International Space Station (ISS) is a product of global collaboration, with components manufactured worldwide. The Russian Orbital Segment modules, including Zarya and Zvezda, were produced at the Khrunichev State Research and Production Space Center in Moscow; Zvezda was originally developed in 1985 as part of the Mir-2 space station, which was never launched. Much of the US Orbital Segment, including the Destiny and Unity modules, the Integrated Truss Structure, and solar arrays, was built at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama and the Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans, with final assembly and launch processing conducted at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The European Space Agency contributed the Columbus module, built in Germany, and Japan contributed the Kibō module, built at the Tsukuba Space Center and the Institute of Space and Astronautical Science, along with the Canadian-built Canadarm2 and Dextre, both a joint Canadian-U.S. effort. All these components were shipped to the Kennedy Space Center for launch processing. Assembly began in November 1998 with the launch of the Russian-built Zarya module on a Proton rocket on 20 November 1998, which provided propulsion, attitude control, communications, and electrical power. Two weeks later, on 4 December 1998, the American-made Unity module was delivered by Space Shuttle Endeavour on STS-88 and joined Zarya, serving as the connection between the Russian and US segments and providing ports for future modules and spacecraft. These initial modules lacked life-support systems, and the ISS remained unmanned for two years while the Russian Mir station was inhabited. The turning point came in July 2000 with the launch of the Zvezda module, which provided living quarters and life-support systems, enabling continuous human presence; the first crew, Expedition 1, arrived in November 2000 aboard Soyuz TM-31. Over the following years, modules were delivered by both Russian rockets and the Space Shuttle. The STS-92 and STS-97 missions added segments of the Integrated Truss Structure, providing Ku band communications, additional attitude control, and solar arrays. A Soyuz-U rocket delivered the Pirs docking compartment, while Space Shuttles Discovery, Atlantis, and Endeavour delivered the Destiny laboratory, Quest airlock, Canadarm2, and additional truss segments. The Space Shuttle Columbia disaster in 2003 grounded the fleet, halting construction; assembly resumed in 2006 with STS-115, which delivered the second set of solar arrays, followed by additional truss segments and arrays on STS-116, STS-117, and STS-118. This expansion allowed for the addition of the US Harmony module, the European Columbus laboratory, and the first two components of the Japanese Kibō laboratory. STS-119 completed the Integrated Truss Structure in March 2009 with the final set of solar arrays; the final section of Kibō was delivered in July 2009 on STS-127, followed by the Poisk module. The US Tranquility module was delivered in February 2010 during STS-130, alongside the Cupola, and the penultimate Russian module, Rassvet, was delivered in May 2010 on STS-132 in exchange for the US-funded Zarya module delivered in 1998. The last pressurized module of the US Orbital Segment, Leonardo, was brought to the station in February 2011 on the final flight of Discovery, STS-133. Russia's new primary research module Nauka docked in July 2021, along with the European Robotic Arm, which can relocate itself to different parts of the Russian modules, and the Prichal module docked in November 2021. As of June 2025, NASA reports that 43 different modules and elements are installed on the ISS. The station functions as a modular space station, allowing for the addition or removal of modules to increase adaptability. Key components include Zarya, the first component of the ISS, launched in 1998, which initially provided power, storage, propulsion, and guidance and now primarily serves as storage; Unity, the first U.S.-built component, constructed by Boeing at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, serves as the connection between the Russian and US segments with six berthing ports; Zvezda, launched in July 2000, is the core of the Russian Orbital Segment, providing living quarters and life-support systems and serving as the command and control center for the Russian segment; Destiny, the primary U.S. research facility, built by Boeing and launched on STS-98, is attached to Unity and supports experiments in medicine, engineering, biotechnology, physics, materials science, and Earth science; the Quest Joint Airlock, launched on STS-104, enables EVAs using either the U.S. EMU or Russian Orlan suits and houses crew and equipment airlocks; Poisk, launched on 10 November 2009, serves as a secondary airlock and supports docking for Soyuz and Progress spacecraft and propellant transfers, and since the departure of Pirs in 2021, it is the sole airlock on the Russian segment; Harmony, launched on STS-120, links the U.S., European, and Japanese modules and provides power, data, and life-support systems, including sleeping quarters for four crew members; Tranquility, launched on STS-130, contains environmental control systems, life-support systems, a toilet, exercise equipment, and an observation cupola; Columbus, the largest single contribution by the European Space Agency, built in Turin, Italy by Thales Alenia Space and integrated in Bremen, Germany, was launched on STS-122 and is controlled from the German Space Operations Center; Kibō, Japan’s research facility, assembled in space over three missions (STS-123, STS-124, STS-127), includes a pressurized lab, an exposed facility, storage, and a robotic arm; the Cupola, launched on STS-130, is an ESA-built observatory module with seven windows for Earth observations, docking, and experiments; Rassvet, delivered on STS-132 in May 2010, is primarily used for cargo storage and as a docking port on the Russian segment and was delivered in exchange for the Zarya module in 1998; the Leonardo Permanent Multipurpose Module, delivered on STS-133 in February 2011, is used for storage of spares, supplies, and waste and serves as the personal hygiene area for astronauts in the US Orbital Segment; the Bigelow Expandable Activity Module (BEAM), developed by Bigelow Aerospace under contract to NASA, arrived on 10 April 2016, was berthed to Tranquility on 16 April 2016, expanded and pressurized on 28 May 2016, and ownership was transferred to NASA in December 2021; the International Docking Adapter (IDA) is a docking system adapter developed to convert APAS-95 to the NASA Docking System (NDS), with two IDAs currently installed on the ISS, originally planned for PMA-2 and PMA-3 at Harmony, with IDA-1 destroyed in a launch incident and IDA-2 installed on PMA-2 on 19 August 2016, while IDA-3 remains planned.

The Expandable Bigelow Advanced Station Enhancement (XBASE) module was planned to be developed by Bigelow Aerospace under a NASA agreement as a ground prototype for a deep space habitation module based on the B330, intended to be attached to the International Space Station. It was proposed in August 2016 as part of the second phase of Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships. However, in March 2020, Bigelow laid off all 88 of its employees, and as of February 2024, the company remains dormant and is considered defunct, making it highly unlikely that the XBASE module will ever be launched. In December 2021, Bigelow Aerospace conveyed ownership of the module to NASA as a result of Bigelow's cessation of activity. The International Docking Adapter (IDA) is a spacecraft docking system adapter developed to convert APAS-95 to the NASA Docking System (NDS), with two IDAs currently installed aboard the ISS. Originally, IDA-1 was planned for PMA-2 at Harmony's forward port and IDA-2 for PMA-3 at Harmony's zenith; after IDA-1 was destroyed in a launch incident, IDA-2 was installed on PMA-2 on 19 August 2016, and IDA-3 was later installed on PMA-3 on 21 August 2019. The NanoRacks Bishop Airlock Module was launched to the ISS on SpaceX CRS-21 on 6 December 2020 and was built by NanoRacks, Thales Alenia Space, and Boeing; it will be used to deploy CubeSats, small satellites, and other external payloads for NASA, CASIS, and other commercial and governmental customers. Nauka, also known as the Multipurpose Laboratory Module, Upgrade, is a Roscosmos-funded component of the ISS launched on 21 July 2021 at 14:58 UTC, successfully docked to Zvezda's nadir port on 29 July 2021 at 13:29 UTC, replacing the Pirs module. In the original ISS plans, Nauka was to use the location of the Docking and Stowage Module (DSM), which was later replaced by the Rassvet module and moved to Zarya's nadir port. Nauka had a temporary docking adapter on its nadir port for crewed and uncrewed missions until Prichal's arrival, when it was removed by a departing Progress spacecraft. Prichal, a 4-tonne (8,800 lb) spherical module launched in November 2021, serves as a docking hub for the Russian segment of the ISS and features six docking ports: forward, aft, port, starboard, zenith, and nadir. One port, equipped with an active hybrid docking system, enabled it to dock with the Nauka module; the remaining five are passive hybrids, allowing docking of Soyuz, Progress, and heavier modules, as well as future spacecraft with modified docking systems. As of 2024, the forward, aft, port, and starboard docking ports remain covered. Prichal was initially intended to be part of the now-canceled Orbital Piloted Assembly and Experiment Complex. The ISS has numerous external components not requiring pressurization, with the largest being the Integrated Truss Structure (ITS), which is 108.5 metres (356 ft) long and consists of ten separate segments, to which the station's main solar arrays and thermal radiators are mounted. The station was originally intended to have six robotic arms, three External Stowage Platforms (ESPs), and four ExPRESS Logistics Carriers (ELCs); these platforms allow experiments such as MISSE, STP-H3, and the Robotic Refueling Mission to be conducted in the vacuum of space by providing electricity and processing data locally, with their primary function being to store spare Orbital Replacement Units (ORUs), including pumps, storage tanks, antennas, and battery units, which are replaced during EVAs or by robotic arms. Several shuttle missions delivered ORUs, including STS-129, STS-133, and STS-134; as of January 2011, only one other mode of ORU transport, the Japanese cargo vessel HTV-2, had been used, delivering an FHRC and CTC-2 via its Exposed Pallet. Smaller exposure facilities are mounted directly to laboratory modules: the Kibō Exposed Facility serves as an external "porch" for the Kibō complex, and a facility on the European Columbus laboratory provides power and data connections for experiments such as the European Technology Exposure Facility and the Atomic Clock Ensemble in Space. The SAGE III-ISS remote sensing instrument was delivered in February 2017 aboard CRS-10, and the NICER experiment was delivered aboard CRS-11 in June 2017. The largest scientific payload externally mounted to the ISS is the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS), a particle physics experiment launched on STS-134 in May 2011 and mounted externally on the ITS to measure cosmic rays for evidence of dark matter and antimatter. The commercial Bartolomeo External Payload Hosting Platform, manufactured by Airbus, was launched on 6 March 2020 aboard CRS-20 and attached to the European Columbus module, providing an additional 12 external payload slots, supplementing the eight on the ExPRESS Logistics Carriers, ten on Kibō, and four on Columbus; it is designed to be robotically serviced and requires no astronaut intervention and is named after Christopher Columbus's younger brother. In May 2010, equipment for Nauka was launched on STS-132 and delivered by Space Shuttle Atlantis, weighing 1.4 metric tons and attached to the outside of Rassvet (MRM-1); it included a spare elbow joint for the European Robotic Arm (ERA), an ERA-portable workpost for EVAs, an RTOd add-on heat radiator, and internal hardware. The RTOd radiator adds additional cooling capability to Nauka, enabling it to host more scientific experiments. The ERA was used to remove the RTOd radiator from Rassvet and transfer it to Nauka during VKD-56, later activated and fully deployed during VKD-58. This process took several months. A portable work platform was transferred to Nauka in August 2023 during VKD-60, which can attach to the end of the ERA to allow cosmonauts to "ride" on the end of the arm during spacewalks. However, six months after outfitting and installation, the RTOd radiator malfunctioned due to a leak, rendering it unusable for Nauka experiments; this is the third ISS radiator leak after Soyuz MS-22 and Progress MS-21 leaks. If a spare RTOd is not available, Nauka experiments will have to rely on Nauka's main launch radiator and the module will never reach its full capacity. Another MLM outfitting is a 4-segment external payload interface called means of attachment of large payloads (Sredstva Krepleniya Krupnogabaritnykh Obyektov, SKKO), delivered in two parts by Progress MS-18 (LCCS part) and Progress MS-21 (SCCCS part) as part of the module activation process, and installed on the ERA aft-facing base point on Nauka during the VKD-55 spacewalk. The Integrated Truss Structure (ITS) serves as a base for the station's primary remote manipulator system, the Mobile Servicing System (MSS), composed of three main components. A grapple fixture was added to Zarya on STS-134 to enable Canadarm2 to inchworm onto the ROS, and during STS-134, the 15 m (50 ft) Orbiter Boom Sensor System (OBSS) was installed, which was used to inspect heat shield tiles on Space Shuttle missions and can now increase the reach of the MSS. Staff on Earth or the ISS can operate the MSS components remotely, performing work outside the station without spacewalks. Japan's Remote Manipulator System, which services the Kibō Exposed Facility, was launched on STS-124 and attached to the Kibō Pressurized Module; it is similar to the Space Shuttle arm and permanently attached at one end with a latching end effector for standard grapple fixtures. The European Robotic Arm, launched alongside the Nauka module, will service the ROS; the ROS does not require spacecraft or modules to be manipulated as all dock automatically and may be discarded the same way. Crew use the two Strela (Russian: Стрела́, lit. 'Arrow') cargo cranes during EVAs for moving crew and equipment around the ROS; each Strela crane has a mass of 45 kg (99 lb). Pirs, launched on 14 September 2001 on a Russian Soyuz-U rocket using a modified Progress spacecraft as an upper stage, was undocked by Progress MS-16 on 26 July 2021 at 10:56 UTC and deorbited at 14:51 UTC to make room for the Nauka module; prior to its departure, it served as the primary Russian airlock, storing and refurbishing Russian Orlan spacesuits. In January 2020, NASA awarded Axiom Space a contract under the NextSTEP2 program to build a commercial module for the ISS, with a firm fixed-price contract to build and deliver the module to the forward port of the Harmony (Node 2) module. Although NASA commissioned only one module, Axiom planned to build a full segment of five modules, including a node module, an orbital research and manufacturing facility, a crew habitat, and a "large-windowed Earth observatory," with the intention of converting the segment into a stand-alone space station after ISS decommissioning in 2030 to serve as a successor. Canadarm2 is planned to continue operations on Axiom Station after the retirement of the ISS in 2030. In December 2024, Axiom revised its plans to require only one module to dock with the ISS before assembling Axiom Station in an independent orbit. As of December 2024, Axiom Space expects to launch the Payload Power Thermal Module (PPTM) to the ISS no earlier than 2027, with PPTM remaining at the ISS until the launch of Axiom's Habitat One (Hab-1) module about one year later, after which it will detach from the ISS to join Hab-1. The US Deorbit Vehicle (USDV) is a NASA-provided spacecraft intended to perform a controlled de-orbit and demise of the station after its operational life ends in 2030. In June 2024, NASA awarded SpaceX a contract to build the Deorbit Vehicle. NASA plans to de-orbit the ISS as soon as it has the "minimum capability" in orbit: "the USDV and at least one commercial station." Several modules were cancelled during the ISS program due to budgetary constraints, becoming unnecessary, or station redesigns after the 2003 Columbia disaster. The US Centrifuge Accommodations Module would have hosted science experiments in varying levels of artificial gravity; the US Habitation Module would have served as the station's living quarters, now spread throughout the station; the US Interim Control Module and ISS Propulsion Module would have replaced Zvezda's functions in case of a launch failure; two Russian Research Modules were planned for scientific research and would have docked to a Russian Universal Docking Module; the Russian Science Power Platform would have supplied power to the Russian Orbital Segment independently of the ITS solar arrays. Science Power Module 1 (SPM-1, also known as NEM-1) and Science Power Module 2 (SPM-2, also known as NEM-2) were originally planned to arrive at the ISS no earlier than 2024 and dock to the Prichal module, which is docked to the Nauka module. In April 2021, Roscosmos announced that NEM-1 would be repurposed to function as the core module of the proposed Russian Orbital Service Station (ROSS), launching no earlier than 2027 and docking to the free-flying Nauka module; NEM-2 may be converted into another core "base" module, to be launched in 2028. The atmosphere on board the ISS is similar to that of Earth, with normal air pressure at 101.3 kPa (14.69 psi), the same as at sea level. The Russian Orbital Segment's life-support systems are contained in the Zvezda service module, with some supplemented by equipment in the USOS; the Nauka laboratory has a complete set of life-support systems. The Elektron system aboard Zvezda and a similar system in Destiny generate oxygen; the crew has a backup option in the form of bottled oxygen and Solid Fuel Oxygen Generation (SFOG) canisters. Carbon dioxide is removed by the Vozdukh system in Zvezda, and other by-products such as methane and ammonia are removed by activated charcoal filters. The ROS atmosphere control system includes triple-redundancy: the Elektron unit, solid fuel generators, and stored oxygen. The primary oxygen supply is from the Elektron unit, which produces O2 and H2 by electrolysis of water and vents H2 overboard; the 1 kW (1.3 hp) system uses approximately one litre of water per crew member per day, which is either brought from Earth or recycled from other systems. Mir was the first spacecraft to use recycled water for oxygen production. The secondary oxygen supply is provided by burning oxygen-producing Vika cartridges; each 'candle' takes 5–20 minutes to decompose at 450–500°C (842–932°F), producing 600 litres (13).

Oxygen and Solid Fuel Oxygen Generation (SFOG) canisters, along with a chemical oxygen generator system, are used to supply oxygen on the International Space Station (ISS). Carbon dioxide is removed by the Vozdukh system in the Zvezda module, while other metabolic by-products such as methane from the intestines and ammonia from sweat are filtered out using activated charcoal. The ROS atmosphere control system includes a primary oxygen supply from the Elektron unit, which produces oxygen and hydrogen via water electrolysis and vents hydrogen overboard, consuming approximately one litre of water per crew member per day—either brought from Earth or recycled. The secondary oxygen supply comes from Vika cartridges, each "candle" producing 600 litres (130 imp gal; 160 US gal) of oxygen over 5–20 minutes at 450–500 °C (842–932 °F), and is manually operated. The US Orbital Segment (USOS) has redundant oxygen supplies, including a pressurized tank on the Quest airlock module delivered in 2001 and later supplemented by the ESA-built Advanced Closed-Loop System (ACLS) in the Tranquility module, which produces oxygen via electrolysis and converts hydrogen with carbon dioxide into water and methane. Double-sided solar arrays provide electrical power, collecting direct sunlight and reflected Earthlight, and are more efficient and operate at lower temperatures than single-sided cells. The Russian segment uses 28 V low-voltage DC from two rotating solar arrays on Zvezda, while the USOS uses 130–180 V DC from its PV arrays, with power stabilized at 160 V DC and converted to 124 V DC for user systems; the higher voltage reduces conductor weight but poses crew safety risks. The USOS solar arrays consist of four wing pairs, totaling 75 to 90 kilowatts, each about 375 m² (4,036 sq ft) and 58 m (190 ft) long, tracking the Sun via alpha and beta gimbals, with Night Glider mode used at night to reduce aerodynamic drag. The station originally used nickel–hydrogen batteries (NiH2) for power during eclipses, with a 6.5-year lifespan and over 37,000 charge/discharge cycles, regularly replaced over the station’s 20-year life; these were replaced in 2016 by lithium-ion batteries, expected to last until the end of the ISS program. The large solar panels create a high voltage difference with the ionosphere, risking arcing and sputtering, mitigated by plasma contactor units that establish current paths to ambient space plasma. A passive thermal control system (PTCS) uses external materials, insulation like MLI, and heat pipes to manage internal heat; if insufficient, an External Active Thermal Control System (EATCS) uses a non-toxic water loop to cool and dehumidify the atmosphere, transferring heat to an external liquid ammonia loop that radiates heat via external radiators, capable of rejecting up to 70 kW—significantly more than the 14 kW of the earlier EEATCS. The ISS uses various radio communication systems for telemetry, scientific data, rendezvous, docking, and crew-to-ground or crew-to-family audio/video links. The Russian segment primarily uses the Lira antenna on Zvezda for direct ground communication and can utilize the Luch data relay system, restored to operation in 2011 and 2012 with Luch-5A and Luch-5B; it also uses the Voskhod-M system for internal telephone and VHF radio links. The USOS uses S-band (on the P1/S1 truss) and Ku-band (on the Z1 truss) systems, routed via the United States Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System (TDRSS) for near-continuous communication with Mission Control Center in Houston. Data for Canadarm2, Columbus, and Kibō were originally routed via these bands, with future support from European and Japanese data relay systems. UHF radio is used during EVAs and for docking/undocking with spacecraft; automated vehicles like the ATV used laser and Proximity Communications Equipment for docking. The USOS has approximately 100 commercial off-the-shelf laptops running Windows or Linux, modified for 28 V DC power and ventilation due to heat buildup; NASA maintains high commonality to allow on-station repairs. Laptops are divided into Portable Computer System (PCS) and Station Support Computers (SSC) types. PCS laptops run Linux and connect to the primary Command & Control computer (C&C MDM), which runs Debian Linux (switched from Windows in 2013), supervising critical station systems; since it has no display or keyboard, astronauts use a PCS laptop via a USB to 1553 adapter as a remote terminal, with failures in 2001, 2007, and 2017, the latter requiring a spacewalk for repair. SSC laptops handle general tasks such as reviewing procedures, managing experiments, email, video chat, and entertainment, connecting via Wi-Fi to the ground through Ku-band; speeds were upgraded from 10 Mbit/s download and 3 Mbit/s upload to 600 Mbit/s in 2019, and crew members have internet access. Each permanent crew is assigned an expedition number, with expeditions lasting up to six months; increments cover the same period but include cargo and activities. Expeditions 1 to 6 had three-person crews; after the Space Shuttle Columbia disaster, Expeditions 7 to 12 were reduced to two-person "caretaker" crews due to limited resupply from Progress; after the Shuttle returned to flight, three-person crews resumed with Expedition 13, expanding to six around 2010, and increasing to seven with the arrival of commercial spacecraft beginning in 2020—matching the original design. Oleg Kononenko of Roscosmos holds the record for the longest time in space and at the ISS, totaling nearly 1,111 days across five long-duration missions (Expedition 17, 30/31, 44/45, 57/58/59, and 69/70/71), and served as commander three times (Expedition 31, 58/59, and 70/71). Peggy Whitson of NASA and Axiom Space has spent the most time in space as an American, accumulating over 675 days on Expeditions 5, 16, 50/51/52 and Axiom Missions 2 and 4. As of June 2023, 13 individuals from 26 countries have paid for their own travel to the ISS, referred to as "spaceflight participants" by Roscosmos and NASA due to professional training and scientific activities, rather than "space tourists." Initially, access was provided by Roscosmos via Soyuz seats at about $40 million through Space Adventures, criticized by NASA and ESA, which resisted training Dennis Tito, the first private visitor. Beginning in 2021, NASA authorized Private Astronaut Missions (PAMs) using NASA-certified U.S. commercial vehicles with a former NASA astronaut as mission commander; the first PAM, Axiom Mission 1, launched in 2022 with one commander and three private passengers, followed by Axiom Mission 2 in 2023 with one private passenger and two Saudi Space Agency astronauts; NASA offers up to two PAMs per year, and PAMs are also used by ESA and other nations for short-term missions. Crewed and uncrewed spacecraft have supported operations, including 93 Progress, 73 Soyuz, 50 SpaceX Dragon, 37 Space Shuttle, 21 Cygnus, 9 HTV, 5 ATV, and 2 Boeing Starliner missions. There are currently eight docking ports, with four additional ports installed but not yet activated; forward and aft ports are at the front and rear, nadir points toward Earth, zenith away from it, port to the left, starboard to the right when facing forward. Cargo spacecraft performing orbital re-boosts typically dock at aft, forward, or nadir ports. As of 27 November 2025, 292 individuals from 26 countries have visited the ISS, including 171 from the United States, 65 from Russia, 11 from Japan, and 9 from Canada; Italy had 6, France and Germany each had 4, Saudi Arabia, Sweden, and UAE each had 2, and one person from each of Belarus, Belgium, Brazil, Denmark, Hungary, India, Israel, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Netherlands, Poland, South Africa, South Korea, Spain, Turkey, and the United Kingdom. Uncrewed missions deliver cargo such as supplies, scientific investigations, spacewalk equipment, hardware, propellant, water, and gases, primarily via Russian Progress, retired European ATV, Japanese HTV, and American Dragon and Cygnus; several Russian modules were launched uncrewed and autonomously docked. Russian spacecraft autonomously rendezvous and dock using the Kurs system, exchanging radio signals with the station’s beacon, with crew supervising and able to intervene via TORU if needed; automated docking began with the Soviet program in 1967, with Kurs introduced on Mir in 1986 and refined since, offering reliability and long-term cost savings. SpaceX Dragon 2 can autonomously rendezvous and dock, with astronauts able to manually fly the vehicle on crewed missions. Other automated spacecraft use a semi-automated process: they approach and park, then are commanded to close in for grappled berthing by the Mobile Servicing System robotic arm; this includes Cygnus and HTV-X; retired Dragon 1, ATV, and HTV used this method. Before docking, navigation and attitude control (GNC) is managed by ground control of the spacecraft’s country, set to allow the station to drift rather than use thrusters or gyroscopes; solar panels are turned edge-on to avoid thruster residue. Prior to retirement, Shuttle launches were often prioritized over Soyuz, with occasional priority given to Soyuz carrying crew or time-critical cargo like biological experiments. Orbital Replacement Units (ORUs) are spare parts such as pumps, storage tanks, controller boxes, antennas, and battery units, stored externally on ExPRESS Logistics Carriers (ELCs) or External Stowage Platforms (ESPs), which also hold science experiments and provide power and local network connections; a major emphasis on stocking ORUs occurred around 2011 before the end of the shuttle program, as commercial vehicles like Cygnus and Dragon carry only one-tenth to one-quarter the payload. Unexpected problems, including an air leak in the USOS in 2004 and fumes from an Elektron oxygen generator, have impacted assembly timelines and work schedules, leading to reduced capabilities and, in some cases, potential abandonment of the station for safety.

Orbital Replacement Units (ORUs) are spare parts that can be easily replaced when a unit reaches the end of its design life or fails. Examples include pumps, storage tanks, controller boxes, antennas, and battery units; some can be replaced using robotic arms. Most ORUs are stored outside the International Space Station (ISS), either on small ExPRESS Logistics Carriers (ELCs) or on larger External Stowage Platforms (ESPs), which also house science experiments. Both ELCs and ESPs provide electricity to components that could be damaged by the cold of space, requiring heating. Larger carriers also feature local area network (LAN) connections for telemetry to link experiments. A major focus on stocking the U.S. segment of the ISS with ORUs occurred around 2011, prior to the end of the NASA shuttle program, as commercial vehicles like Cygnus and Dragon carry only one-tenth to one-quarter the payload capacity. Unexpected failures have disrupted the station’s assembly timeline and work schedules, leading to reduced capabilities and, in some cases, potential abandonment for safety. Notable incidents include an air leak in the U.S. segment in 2004, fumes from an Elektron oxygen generator in 2006, and a 2007 computer failure in the Russian Orbital Segment (ROS) during STS-117, which disabled environmental control systems including thrusters and the Elektron, due to condensation in electrical connectors causing a short circuit. During STS-120 in 2007, after relocating the P6 truss and solar arrays, it was discovered that the solar array had torn and failed to deploy properly. Astronauts Scott Parazynski and Douglas Wheelock conducted an EVA with precautions to avoid electric shock due to sunlight exposure. The same year, the starboard Solar Alpha Rotary Joint (SARJ) experienced excessive vibration and high-current spikes, leading to a decision to limit its motion. EVAs on STS-120 and STS-123 revealed metallic shavings and damage to bearing surfaces, prompting the joint to be locked. Repairs were completed during STS-126 with lubrication and replacement of 11 out of 12 trundle bearings. In September 2008, damage to the S1 radiator was first observed in Soyuz imagery, showing a peeled sub-panel likely from a micro-meteoroid or debris impact. On 15 May 2009, a computer-controlled valve shut off the ammonia tubing and vented the ammonia from the panel, eliminating a leak risk. A Service Module thruster cover struck the S1 radiator during an EVA in 2008, but its impact remains undetermined. On 1 August 2010, a failure in cooling Loop A (starboard side) left the station with only half its normal cooling capacity and no redundancy, due to a problem in the ammonia pump module. Several subsystems, including two of four Control Moment Gyroscopes (CMGs), were shut down. Planned operations were interrupted by a series of EVAs: a first EVA on 7 August 2010 to replace the pump module was incomplete due to an ammonia leak in one of four quick-disconnects; a second EVA on 11 August successfully removed the failed module; a third EVA restored Loop A to normal function. The U.S. segment’s cooling system is primarily built by Boeing, which also manufactured the failed pump. The four Main Bus Switching Units (MBSUs), located in the S0 truss, control power routing from the solar array wings to the rest of the station. Each MBSU has two power channels feeding 160V DC to two DC-to-DC power converters (DDCUs) that supply 124V power. In late 2011, MBSU-1 stopped responding to commands or sending health data, though it still routed power correctly. It was scheduled for replacement during the next EVA, with a spare already on board. A planned EVA on 30 August 2012 failed when a bolt jammed before securing the electrical connection. The loss of MBSU-1 reduced station power to 75%, requiring operational limitations until resolved. On 5 September 2012, astronauts Sunita Williams and Akihiko Hoshide successfully replaced MBSU-1 and restored full power. On 24 December 2013, astronauts installed a new ammonia pump after a prior failure halted science experiments; they faced a "mini blizzard" of ammonia during the installation, making it the second Christmas Eve spacewalk in NASA history. The ISS is operated and monitored by its respective space agencies at mission control centers worldwide, primarily the Christopher C. Kraft Jr. Mission Control Center in Houston and the RKA Mission Control Center (TsUP) in Moscow, with support from Tsukuba Space Center in Japan, Payload Operations and Integration Center in Huntsville, Alabama, Columbus Control Center in Munich, Germany, and Mobile Servicing System Control at the Canadian Space Agency’s headquarters in Saint-Hubert, Quebec. The ISS maintains a nearly circular orbit with a minimum mean altitude of 370 km (230 mi) and a maximum of 460 km (290 mi), at an inclination of 51.6 degrees to Earth’s equator and an eccentricity of 0.0002267, selected because it is the lowest inclination reachable by Russian Soyuz and Progress spacecraft launched from Baikonur without overflying China or dropping spent stages in inhabited areas. It travels at 28,000 km/h (17,000 mph), completing 15.5 orbits per day (93 minutes per orbit). Altitude was lowered during NASA shuttle flights to allow heavier payloads, and after shuttle retirement, the nominal orbit was raised from about 350 km to about 400 km. Other supply vehicles do not require such adjustments. Atmospheric drag reduces altitude by about 2 km per month on average. Orbital boosts are performed using the Zvezda service module’s main engines or docked Russian or European spacecraft; the Automated Transfer Vehicle can be modified to add a second docking port. A boost takes about two orbits (three hours) to complete, using approximately 7.5 tonnes of chemical fuel annually at a cost of about $210 million. The Russian Orbital Segment contains the Data Management System (DMS), which handles Guidance, Navigation, and Control (ROS GNC). Initially, Zarya controlled the station, but after Zvezda docked, control was transferred to Zvezda, which uses the ESA-built DMS-R. The ROS uses two fault-tolerant computers (FTCs), each with three identical processing units working in parallel and using majority voting for fault masking. Zvezda uses gyroscopes (reaction wheels) and thrusters for attitude control; gyroscopes store momentum without propellant, and thrusters are used when gyroscopes saturate. In February 2005, during Expedition 10, an incorrect command used about 14 kg of propellant before being corrected. When ROS and USOS attitude control computers fail to communicate, a rare "force fight" can occur where the ROS GNC overrides the USOS, which lacks thrusters. Docked spacecraft can also assist in maintaining station attitude, such as during the installation of the S3/S4 truss. The ISS orbits at low altitudes where space debris is common, including spent rocket stages, defunct satellites, explosion fragments, paint flakes, solid rocket motor slag, and coolant from US-A nuclear-powered satellites, along with natural micrometeoroids. Larger debris can be tracked and is less dangerous; however, objects from 1 cm down to microscopic size number in the trillions and pose a threat due to kinetic energy and trajectory. Spacewalkers are at risk of suit damage and exposure to vacuum. Ballistic panels, or micrometeorite shielding, protect pressurized sections and critical systems. On the US segment, Whipple Shields consist of an inner 1.5–5.0 cm aluminum layer, a 10 cm Kevlar and Nextel intermediate layer, and an outer stainless steel layer that shatters incoming objects into a cloud, spreading impact energy. On the ROS, a carbon fiber reinforced polymer honeycomb screen is spaced from the hull, followed by an aluminum honeycomb screen, thermal insulation, and glass cloth. Space debris is tracked from the ground, and crew are notified. If necessary, thrusters on the ROS can alter the station’s orbit to avoid debris. These Debris Avoidance Manoeuvres (DAMs) are common, with ten performed by the end of 2009; typically, a velocity increase of 1 m/s raises the orbit by one to two kilometers. Lowering altitude is possible but wastes propellant. If a threat is identified too late, the crew closes all hatches and retreats to their spacecraft for evacuation. Partial evacuations occurred on 13 March 2009, 28 June 2011, 24 March 2012, 16 June 2015, November 2021, and 27 June 2024. The November 2021 evacuation was triggered by a Russian anti-satellite weapon test; NASA administrator Bill Nelson stated it was unthinkable that Russia would endanger lives on the ISS. The ISS is visible to the naked eye as a bright white, moving dot during twilight, after sunset, or before sunrise when it is sunlit and outside Earth’s shadow, crossing the sky at mid-latitudes. It appears for up to 10 minutes and is visible from 95% of inhabited land, but not from extreme northern or southern latitudes. Under specific conditions—mid-latitude observer, near solstice, and ISS passing toward the pole near midnight—it can be observed on five consecutive orbits. A "Spot the Station" service launched by NASA in November 2012 sends text and email alerts when the station will pass over a user’s location. Using telescopes or binoculars, the ISS can be viewed during daylight; amateur astronomers also observe transits of the ISS in front of the Sun, especially during eclipses. Gravity at ISS altitude is about 90% of Earth’s surface gravity, but apparent weightlessness results from continuous freefall. This state is disturbed by five effects. The ISS is partially shielded by Earth’s magnetic field, which deflects solar wind from about 70,000 km above Earth’s surface; solar flares remain a hazard with only a few minutes’ warning. In 2005, during an X-3 class solar flare, Expedition 10 crew took shelter in a shielded part of the ROS. Outside Earth’s atmosphere, ISS crew receive about one millisievert of radiation per day (equivalent to a year’s natural exposure on Earth), increasing cancer risk. Radiation damages lymphocyte DNA and chromosomes, contributing to lower astronaut immunity, and is linked to higher cataract incidence. Protective shielding and medications help reduce these risks. Radiation levels on the ISS range from 12 to 28.8 milli rads per day, about five times higher than for airline passengers and crew due to the absence of Earth’s electromagnetic field.

In 2005, during the initial "proton storm" of an X-3 class solar flare, the crew of Expedition 10 took shelter in a more heavily shielded section of the Russian Orbital Segment (ROS) designed for such events. Subatomic charged particles, mainly protons from cosmic rays and solar wind, are normally absorbed by Earth's atmosphere; when their concentration is high enough, they produce visible auroras. Outside Earth's atmosphere, ISS crew are exposed to about one millisievert per day—equivalent to a full year's natural background radiation on Earth—increasing their cancer risk. Radiation can penetrate living tissue and damage the DNA and chromosomes of lymphocytes, which are vital to the immune system, potentially contributing to reduced immunity in astronauts. It has also been linked to a higher incidence of cataracts. Protective measures such as shielding and medications help reduce these risks to acceptable levels. Radiation levels on the ISS range from 12 to 28.8 milli rads per day, about five times higher than those experienced by airline passengers and crew, as Earth's electromagnetic field offers nearly the same protection in low Earth orbit as in the stratosphere. For instance, a 12-hour flight exposes a passenger to 0.1 millisieverts or 0.2 millisieverts per day—just one-fifth of the rate for an astronaut in low Earth orbit—and this exposure occurs only during a few hours, whereas ISS crew are exposed continuously during their stay. Hazardous molds that can clog air and water filters may develop on space stations, producing acids that degrade metal, glass, and rubber and posing health risks to crew. To address this, the LOCAD-PTS portable test system was developed to identify common bacteria and molds faster than traditional culturing methods, which require sample return to Earth. In 2018, researchers detected five Enterobacter bugandensis strains on the ISS (none of which are pathogenic to humans), prompting a call for careful monitoring of microorganisms to maintain a medically safe environment. Contamination is prevented through reduced humidity, mold-killing paint, antiseptic solutions, and all materials used in the ISS being tested for fungal resistance. Since 2016, ESA-sponsored experiments under the "Microbial Aerosol Tethering on Innovative Surfaces" (MATISS) program have tested anti-bacterial materials to develop "smart surfaces" that inhibit bacterial growth. The program involves deploying small plaques with glass squares coated with different materials, which remain on the station for six months before return. The final experiment, launched on 5 June 2023 aboard the SpaceX CRS-28 cargo mission, included four plaques; two were returned after eight months and two after 16 months. Previous experiments used only light microscopy, while this one used pure silica quartz glass for spectrographic analysis. In April 2019, NASA reported a 14-month study on microorganisms and fungi across three ISS missions, sampling eight predefined locations and using molecular-based methods in addition to culturing, resulting in a more complete microbial catalog. This study improved understanding of closed environments like pharmaceutical clean rooms. Spaceflight is not quiet; noise levels exceed acoustic standards dating back to the Apollo missions. NASA and ISS partners, through the Multilateral Medical Operations Panel (MMOP) Acoustics Subgroup, have established noise control and hearing loss prevention goals since the station's early operations. While noise levels rarely exceed 85 dBA—below OSHA thresholds—they are present 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with missions averaging six months in duration. These levels interfere with sleep, communication, and alarm audibility. Over 19 years, significant efforts have been made to reduce noise, including setting acoustic limits, selecting quiet payloads, conducting pre-launch tests, and monitoring in-flight sound levels. As new modules and spacecraft are added, the Acoustics Subgroup has implemented acoustic covers, absorptive materials, noise barriers, and vibration isolators. When pumps and fans age and become noisier, the group has recommended replacing them with quieter technologies. NASA uses conservative damage risk criteria based on NIOSH and WHO recommendations, applying terrestrial hearing loss prevention methods. The Noise Exposure Estimation Tool (NEET) calculates task-based noise exposure to determine when hearing protection devices (HPDs) are needed, with guidance documented in the Noise Hazard Inventory for crew reference. The group also tracks noise exceedances, applies engineering controls, and monitors hearing thresholds on orbit. There have been no persistent mission-related hearing threshold shifts among US Orbital Segment crew (JAXA, CSA, ESA, NASA) over nearly 20 years of operations, or nearly 175,000 work hours. In 2020, the MMOP Acoustics Subgroup received the Safe-In-Sound Award for Innovation. Ammonia, used in the station's external radiators, could potentially leak into pressurized modules. In April 2019, NASA reported results from the Astronaut Twin Study, in which astronaut Scott Kelly spent a year in space while his identical twin remained on Earth, revealing long-term changes in DNA and cognition. In November 2019, researchers reported that astronauts experienced serious blood flow and clot problems during a six-month study of 11 healthy astronauts, findings that may impact long-duration missions, including to Mars. Psychosocial stressors are among the most significant factors affecting crew morale and performance. Cosmonaut Valery Ryumin noted in his journal during a stay on Salyut 6 that "all the conditions necessary for murder are met" if two men are confined in an 18-foot by 20-foot cabin for two months. NASA's interest in psychological stress began with early missions and was renewed when US astronauts joined cosmonauts on Mir; common stressors included public scrutiny and isolation from family, which remains a concern on the ISS, such as when Daniel Tani's mother died in a car accident or when Michael Fincke missed the birth of his second child. A study of the longest spaceflight found that the first three weeks are critical, as attention is adversely affected during environmental adaptation. ISS crew flights typically last five to six months. The working environment includes stress from living in cramped quarters with crew from diverse cultures who speak different languages; first-generation stations had single-language crews, while current stations have multilingual crews who must speak English and Russian. In microgravity, crew members often feel upside down and struggle with distance perception, leading to disorientation, getting lost, pulling switches incorrectly, or misjudging vehicle approach speeds. Long-term weightlessness causes muscle atrophy, osteopenia, fluid redistribution, cardiovascular slowing, reduced red blood cell production, balance disorders, and weakened immunity, with minor symptoms including weight loss and facial puffiness. Sleep is frequently disturbed by mission activities, spacecraft arrivals/departures, and high sound levels, as the atmosphere cannot naturally thermosiphon, requiring constant fan operation. To counteract these effects, the station has two TVIS treadmills (including the COLBERT), the ARED (Advanced Resistive Exercise Device) for weightlifting without increasing bone density, and a stationary bicycle; each astronaut exercises at least two hours per day. Astronauts use bungee cords to secure themselves to treadmills. The living and working space on the ISS is larger than a six-bedroom house, featuring seven private sleeping quarters, three bathrooms, two dining rooms, a gym, and a panoramic 360-degree-view bay window. Dedicated crew quarters are located in Zvezda (two), Nauka (one), and Harmony (four); these soundproof, person-sized booths offer privacy, ventilation, and amenities like sleeping bags, reading lamps, and storage. Visiting crew use tethered sleeping bags attached to walls or their spacecraft, avoiding free-floating sleep to prevent equipment collisions. Proper ventilation is essential to prevent oxygen deprivation from carbon dioxide buildup. The station's lighting is adjustable for dimming, turning off, and color temperature changes to support work and rest. The ISS operates on Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). A typical day begins at 06:00 with wake-up, post-sleep routines, and a morning inspection; after breakfast, the crew holds a daily planning conference starting at 08:10. Morning tasks include exercise, experiments, maintenance, or operations. A one-hour lunch break occurs at 13:05, followed by afternoon work and exercise. Pre-sleep activities, including dinner and a crew conference, begin at 19:30, with sleep starting at 21:30. Crew work about 10 hours on weekdays and 5 hours on Saturdays, with the rest allocated to relaxation or catching up on tasks. Free time includes hobbies, family communication, or gazing at Earth. TV is available on board. When the Space Shuttle was active, ISS crews aligned with the shuttle's Mission Elapsed Time. To simulate night, station windows are covered during sleep periods, as the ISS experiences 16 sunrises and sunsets daily. Individual and crew characteristics are reflected in station decor and expressions, such as religion, which has created a material exchange between the ISS and Russia. The micro-society, including potential distinct station cultures, is studied through art, dust accumulation, and archaeological analysis of discarded materials. Food on the ISS is preserved and packaged for long storage, minimal waste, and system protection; due to microgravity, taste is dulled, so meals are seasoned more heavily. Crews look forward to resupply missions that deliver fresh fruit and vegetables. To prevent crumbs and spills, foods are in specialized packaging, liquid condiments are preferred over powders, and containers are secured with Velcro or magnets. Drinks are delivered as powders to mix with water, soups and beverages are sipped from plastic bags with straws, and solid foods are eaten with utensils attached to trays by magnets, with any food waste collected to avoid clogging filters. The first galley was installed in Zvezda, with an electro-resistive can warmer and water dispenser for hot and ambient water; many Russian meals are in cans or retort pouches. A second galley was added to Unity, containing two briefcase-shaped food warmers, a refrigerator (added in 2008), and a water dispenser. Most U.S. food is in retort pouches, rehydrated and heated or chilled as desired. Crews occasionally gather for group meals, especially during holidays, but more often eat in small groups due to differing schedules. Russian cosmonauts can dine separately in Zvezda using the can warmer. With the growing diversity of NASA's astronaut corps and the large number of international astronauts, food variety has expanded significantly, with meals reflecting cultural backgrounds and personal preferences, often shared among crew. Experiments have grown fresh vegetables in orbit, including three types of lettuce, Chinese cabbage, mizuna mustard, and red Russian kale; some are eaten by crew, others returned to Earth for analysis. NASA plans to grow tomatoes, peppers, and eventually berries, beans, and other nutrient-rich foods, which could improve nutrition and possibly offer radiation protection. The ISS has three Russian-designed toilets in Zvezda, Tranquility, and Nauka. Inside the "Waste and Hygiene Compartments," occupants fasten to the seat with spring-loaded bars for a proper seal; a lever activates a fan that opens a suction port to remove waste. Solid waste is stored in individual bags in an aluminum container, later transferred to cargo spacecraft that burn up on reentry. Liquid waste is collected via a hose with anatomically shaped funnel adapters for both men and women; urine is processed by the Water Recovery System into drinking water. Showers were first introduced in the 1970s on Skylab and Salyut 3, but crews found them complex and problematic.

The International Space Station (ISS) is equipped with three Russian-designed toilets located in the Zvezda, Tranquility, and Nauka modules. Inside these Waste and Hygiene Compartments, astronauts secure themselves to the toilet seat using spring-loaded restraining bars to ensure a proper seal. A lever activates a powerful fan that opens a suction port at the bottom of the bowl, carrying waste away; solid waste is stored in individual bags within an aluminum container and later transferred to cargo spacecraft that burn up upon reentry, while liquid waste is collected via a hose with anatomically shaped funnel adapters for both men and women. Urine is diverted to the Water Recovery System, where it is processed into drinking water. Showers were first introduced in the early 1970s on Skylab and Salyut 3, but due to complexity, were reduced to a monthly activity by the early 1980s on Salyut 6; the ISS, like later Russian stations, has no shower, and astronauts clean themselves with wet wipes, a water jet, and soap from a toothpaste-like tube, using rinseless shampoo and edible toothpaste to conserve water. Originally intended for a 15-year mission, the ISS has been repeatedly extended due to its success and support, with its oldest modules now in orbit for over 20 years and reliability having decreased. It has been proposed to redirect funds to a return to the Moon, and under the Outer Space Treaty, launching parties are legally responsible for their spacecraft or modules. Russia has stated it plans to exit the ISS program after 2025, though its modules will provide orbital station-keeping until 2028. The U.S. initially planned to deorbit the ISS in 2016, but in September 2015, Boeing’s contract with NASA was extended to September 2020, including extending the station’s primary structural hardware to the end of 2028. The Space Frontier Act of 2018 aimed to extend operations to 2030 and passed the Senate but failed in the U.S. House; the Leading Human Spaceflight Act was introduced with the same intent and confirmed in December 2018; Congress later passed similar provisions in the CHIPS and Science Act, signed into law by President Joe Biden on 9 August 2022. NASA has suggested extending ISS operations beyond 2030 if Commercial LEO Destinations providers cannot meet NASA’s needs. NASA considered disposal options including natural orbital decay, reboosting, or a controlled deorbit to a remote ocean area, but rejected random reentry due to debris risks and reboosting due to cost and hazards. Prior to 2010, a modified Progress spacecraft was considered for deorbit, but NASA concluded it was inadequate and opted for a dedicated vehicle. In January 2022, NASA announced a planned deorbit in January 2031 using the "U.S. Deorbit Vehicle," with remnants directed to the South Pacific Ocean "spacecraft cemetery." The deorbit vehicle will be launched in 2030, docked at the Harmony forward port, remain dormant for about a year as the orbit naturally decays to 220 km (140 mi), then conduct one or more orientation burns to lower the perigee to 150 km (93 mi), followed by a final deorbit burn. NASA began planning the deorbit vehicle after concerns about Russia’s potential abrupt withdrawal, leaving partners with limited options for a controlled reentry. In June 2024, NASA selected SpaceX to develop the U.S. Deorbit Vehicle, a contract worth up to $843 million, consisting of a modified Cargo Dragon spacecraft paired with a lengthened trunk module equipped with 46 Draco thrusters (instead of the normal 16) and carrying 30,000 kg (66,000 lb) of propellant—nearly six times the normal load. NASA is still working to secure funding for the vehicle’s development, launch, and operation. On 20 February 2025, Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Senior Advisor to President Trump, suggested in a tweet that the ISS be de-orbited "two years from now," stating it has "served its purpose" and "very little incremental utility," though no official decision to accelerate the deorbit has been made. The follow-up to NASA’s strategy is the Commercial LEO Destinations Program, which will allow private companies to build and maintain their own stations, with NASA procuring access starting in 2028. The European Space Agency is also seeking private space stations for orbital services and material retrieval from the ISS. Axiom Station is planned to begin as a single module temporarily hosted at the ISS in 2027. There have been suggestions in the commercial space industry that the ISS could be converted to commercial operations after retirement, including as a space hotel. Russia previously planned to use its orbital segment for the OPSEK station after the ISS is decommissioned, with the Multipurpose Laboratory Module (Nauka; MLM), launched in July 2021, and other new Russian modules under consideration for removal—these modules were still within their useful lives in 2024. In 2011, the Exploration Gateway Platform concept proposed using leftover U.S. Orbital Segment (USOS) hardware and Zvezda 2 as a refueling depot at an Earth–Moon Lagrange point, though the entire USOS was not designed for disassembly and will be discarded. In 2022, companies like CisLunar proposed repurposing ISS components or using space debris for raw materials or fuel instead of ocean disposal. In July 2024, NASA stated it had not seen any viable proposals for reusing the ISS or its parts. The ISS is considered the most expensive single item ever constructed, with a total cost of US$150 billion as of 2010, including NASA’s $58.7 billion (adjusted to $89.73 billion in 2021 dollars) from 1985 to 2015, Russia’s $12 billion, Europe’s $5 billion, Japan’s $5 billion, Canada’s $2 billion, and $50.4 billion from 36 shuttle flights at $1.4 billion each. Assuming 20,000 man-days of use from 2000 to 2015 by crews of two to six people, each man-day cost $7.5 million—less than half the inflation-adjusted $19.6 million ($5.5 million before inflation) per man-day of Skylab. The ISS has become an international symbol of human cooperation and scientific achievement, representing a cooperative international approach rather than a commercialized or militarized interplanetary future. It has been featured in numerous documentaries, including the IMAX film Space Station 3D (2002) and A Beautiful Planet (2016), and films such as Apogee of Fear (2012), Yolki 5 (2016), The Day After Tomorrow (2004), Love (2011), Gravity (2013) with the Chinese Tiangong 1, Life (2017), and I.S.S. (2023). In 2022, The Challenge (Doctor's House Call) was filmed aboard the ISS and marked the first feature film in which both professional actors and a director worked together in space. Neal Stephenson’s 2015 novel Seveneves is set largely on the ISS in its first two parts, depicting it as it existed at the time with a large captured asteroid attached. Samantha Harvey’s 2023 novel Orbital is set on the ISS and won the 2024 Booker Prize. Ceridwen Dovey’s 2024 short story collection Only the Astronauts, in which each narrator is an inanimate object in space, includes the ISS. In Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the ISS is destroyed during the "Second Sun" mission when Captain Price launches an ICBM into the atmosphere, creating a shockwave. In Far Cry New Dawn, the ISS is present as an expedition site that has fallen to Earth during a nuclear war.
